kcet|Physics|2017|12|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
In **uniform** circular motion the speed never changes, so the acceleration can have no
component along the motion — it must be entirely **perpendicular** to it.
**Step 1 — locate the velocity.** The velocity is always **tangential** to the circle ✓
**Step 2 — locate the acceleration.** With the speed constant, the only acceleration is
the **centripetal** one, directed along the radius **towards the centre** ✓
**Step 3 — find the angle.** A radius and the tangent at the same point meet at a right
angle, so
**θ = 90°** ✓
**Why it must be exactly 90°.** Resolve the acceleration into a component along the
velocity and one perpendicular to it:
the **parallel** component changes the **speed**
the **perpendicular** component changes the **direction**
"Uniform" means the speed is constant, so the parallel component is **zero** ✓ and the
acceleration is wholly perpendicular.
**Confirming with the work-energy theorem.** The kinetic energy is constant, so the net
force does no work:
W = F̄·d̄ = Fd cos θ = 0
Since F ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0, we need **cos θ = 0**, that is **θ = 90°** ✓
**Confirming by differentiation.** With r̄ = r(cos ωt, sin ωt):
v̄ = rω(−sin ωt, cos ωt)
ā = −rω²(cos ωt, sin ωt)
and their dot product is
v̄·ā = r²ω³(sin ωt cos ωt − cos ωt sin ωt) = **0** ✓ perpendicular at every instant.
**Reading the distractors.**
**180°** ✗ would mean the acceleration directly opposes the velocity — that is pure
**deceleration** along a straight line, which would slow the body down, contradicting
"uniform".
**0°** would mean pure speeding up — also excluded.
**45°** and **60°** ✗ would each give a non-zero component along the motion, so the speed
would change ✗ They describe **non-uniform** circular motion, where a tangential
acceleration exists alongside the centripetal one.
**The contrast worth noting.** In **non-uniform** circular motion the total acceleration
has both components and the angle lies strictly between 0° and 180°, varying as the body
speeds up or slows. Only when the speed is constant is the angle pinned at exactly 90° ✓
∴ 90°.
kcet|Physics|2006|2|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
**Displacement** depends only on the start and finish; **average speed** uses the whole
path length.
**Step 1 — find the net displacement.** The cyclist begins at the centre **O** and ends
at the centre **O**, so the straight-line distance between start and finish is
**zero** ✓
**Step 2 — find the total distance travelled.** From the figure the path is
**O to P**, a radius: **1 km**
**P to Q**, a quarter of the circumference (P on the right, Q at the top):
(1/4)(2πr) = (1/4)(2π) = **π/2 km**
**Q to O**, a radius: **1 km**
total = 1 + π/2 + 1 = **(4 + π)/2 km**
**Step 3 — convert the time.**
10 minutes = 10/60 = **1/6 hour**
**Step 4 — compute the average speed.**
average speed = distance/time
= [(4 + π)/2] ÷ (1/6)
= 3(4 + π)
= 3(7·1416)
= **21·4 km/h** ✓
so the pair is **0 and 21·4** ✓
**The distinction being tested.** Average **velocity** would be displacement/time =
0/(1/6) = **0**, while average **speed** is path length/time = **21·4 km/h** ✓ The two
differ whenever the path is not a straight line, and here they differ as starkly as
possible, since the journey returns to its start.
**Checking the distance.** (4 + π)/2 = (4 + 3·1416)/2 = **3·571 km** in ten minutes. At
that rate an hour would cover 6 × 3·571 = **21·4 km** ✓
**Why the quarter circle.** The figure shows P on the circle due **east** of O and Q due
**north**, so the arc PQ subtends a right angle at the centre — one quarter of the full
circumference ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**0, 1** ✗ pairs the right displacement with a speed of 1 km/h, which would need the trip
to take over three hours.
**(π + 4)/2, 0** ✗ has the two **swapped**: (π+4)/2 = 3·571 is the **distance in km**, not
a displacement, and the speed is certainly not zero.
**21·4, (π + 4)/2** ✗ swaps them the other way.
Only one option puts **0** first ✓ and recognising that a round trip has zero
displacement settles the question before any arithmetic.
∴ 0, 21·4.
kcet|Physics|2010|4|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
Velocities add as vectors, and here the two are **equal and opposite** — so they cancel
exactly.
**Step 1 — set a sign convention.** Take the train's direction of motion as **positive**.
velocity of the train relative to the ground: **+2 m s⁻¹**
velocity of the passenger relative to the train: **−2 m s⁻¹** (walking towards the back,
against the train's motion)
**Step 2 — add them.**
v(passenger, ground) = v(passenger, train) + v(train, ground)
= (−2) + (+2)
= **0** ✓
**Step 3 — interpret.** To the observer on the platform the passenger is **stationary** ✓
The passenger walks backwards through the carriage at exactly the rate the carriage
carries them forward, so their position relative to the ground never changes.
**A picture to hold on to.** The passenger stays level with the same lamp-post on the
platform throughout, strolling towards the back of the train while the train slides
forward beneath them ✓ From the platform, they appear to be walking on the spot.
**The relative-velocity rule.** For any three objects,
**v_(A,C) = v_(A,B) + v_(B,C)**
with the inner labels matching and cancelling. Here A = passenger, B = train, C = ground ✓
Getting the **signs** right is the only difficulty, and the phrase "in the opposite
direction of the motion of the train" fixes the passenger's as negative.
**Reading the distractors.**
**4 m s⁻¹** ✗ comes from **adding** the magnitudes, 2 + 2 — correct only if the passenger
walked **towards the front**, in the same direction as the train.
**2 m s⁻¹** ✗ is the speed relative to the **train**, or the train's own speed — not the
combination.
**2 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction** ✗ is the passenger's velocity as seen **from inside
the train**, which is what the question deliberately does not ask ✓
**A check on all four cases.** With the train at +2:
passenger walks forward at 2 → ground sees **+4**
passenger stands still → ground sees **+2**
passenger walks backward at 2 → ground sees **0** ✓ our case
passenger walks backward at 4 → ground sees **−2**
Only the exact cancellation gives zero, and the question's equal speeds are chosen to
produce it ✓
∴ zero.
kcet|Physics|2019|9|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
The block stays on the piston only while the piston's downward acceleration never exceeds
**g** — and that acceleration is greatest at the **top** of the oscillation.
**Step 1 — see where contact is most at risk.** At the highest point the piston
decelerates downward with magnitude ω²A. The block is held down only by gravity, so the
greatest downward acceleration it can follow is **g** ✓ Beyond that the piston drops away
faster than the block can fall and they separate.
**Step 2 — write the condition.**
ω²A ≤ g
so the maximum amplitude is
**A = g/ω²**
**Step 3 — find ω from the frequency.**
ω = 2πf = 2π(0·5) = **π rad s⁻¹**
**Step 4 — substitute.**
A = 9·8/π²
= 9·8/9·87
= **0·993 ≈ 1 m** ✓
**Why the mass is irrelevant.** At the point of separation the normal force is zero, so
the block is in **free fall** — and free fall is the same for every mass ✓ The 10 kg is a
red herring, offered to see whether the reasoning is understood.
**Deriving the condition properly.** For the block on the piston at the top of the
stroke, taking downward as positive:
mg − N = mω²A
so
N = m(g − ω²A)
Contact requires **N ≥ 0**, hence **ω²A ≤ g** ✓ and the mass m cancels from the
inequality entirely.
**Checking with g = 10.** A = 10/π² = **1·013 m** — still essentially **1 m** ✓ so the
answer is insensitive to which value of g is used, another sign that 1 m is intended.
**Reading the distractors.**
**1·5 m** ✗ would give ω²A = π²(1·5) = **14·8 m s⁻²**, greater than g, so the block would
leave the piston ✗
**0·1 m** and **0·5 m** ✗ are safe but not **maximum** — the question asks for the largest
amplitude that still maintains contact, and both leave room to spare (ω²A = 0·99 and
4·9 m s⁻², well under g) ✓
**The physical picture.** Shake a tray up and down slowly and a coin on it stays put;
shake it hard enough and the coin starts to bounce. The threshold is exactly where the
tray's peak downward acceleration reaches g ✓ Here that happens at an amplitude of about
a metre, because the frequency is low — only half a cycle per second.
∴ 1 m.
kcet|Physics|2009|7|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
Mixing two quantities of the **same** liquid means the final temperature is simply the
**weighted average**, with the volumes as weights.
**Step 1 — note what cancels.** Both samples are water, so they share the same density ρ
and specific heat capacity c. The masses are therefore proportional to the **volumes**:
m₁ ∝ 0·1 m³ and m₂ ∝ 0·3 m³ ✓
**Step 2 — write the heat balance.** Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the
cold:
m₁c(80 − T) = m₂c(T − 60)
and since c and ρ cancel throughout:
0·1(80 − T) = 0·3(T − 60)
**Step 3 — expand and solve.**
8 − 0·1T = 0·3T − 18
8 + 18 = 0·3T + 0·1T
26 = 0·4T
**T = 65°C** ✓
**The weighted-average shortcut.**
T = (V₁T₁ + V₂T₂)/(V₁ + V₂)
= (0·1 × 80 + 0·3 × 60)/(0·1 + 0·3)
= (8 + 18)/0·4
= **65°C** ✓ in one line.
**Why the answer is nearer 60 than 80.** There is **three times** as much cold water as
hot, so the mixture settles much closer to the cold temperature ✓ The final value must lie
strictly between 60 and 80, and the 3 : 1 weighting pulls it a quarter of the way up from
60: 60 + (1/4)(20) = **65°C** ✓
**Checking the energy balance.** Taking ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹:
hot water loses 100 kg × 4200 × 15 = **6·3 MJ**
cold water gains 300 kg × 4200 × 5 = **6·3 MJ** ✓ equal, as they must be.
**Reading the distractors.**
**70°C** ✗ is the **unweighted** average of 60 and 80 — right only if the two volumes
were equal, and the commonest error here ✓ The question gives unequal volumes precisely
to test that.
**60°C** ✗ would require the hot water to contribute nothing.
**75°C** ✗ lies above the midpoint, which would need **more** hot water than cold — the
opposite of what is given.
**A sanity check in one step.** The answer must lie between 60 and 80, and below 70 since
cold water predominates ✓ Only 65 satisfies both.
∴ 65°C.
